title: Gear & Your Motorcycle
summary: Before a trip, check the bike's equipment, get familiar with the machine, use face and eye protection, and wear proper gear.
Massachusetts law sets minimum equipment standards, and the operator must keep all safety equipment, including the horn, rearview mirror, fenders, muffler, brakes, and lights, in good working order.
The front needs a properly aimed white headlight; the rear needs a red taillight, a stoplight, and a white plate light, and a sidecar needs a white forward light.

Every bike needs a secure seat for its operator, and one set up for passengers also needs a secure passenger seat and separate footpegs. On any bike, handlebars may not rise above the operator's shoulders when properly seated.

Helmets are mandatory for both riders and passengers in Massachusetts. They prevent brain injury about 67% of the time, and NHTSA credits them with saving hundreds of riders' lives each year; mile for mile, riders are more likely than car passengers to die in a crash.
Every motorcycle helmet sold in the U.S. must meet Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard (FMVSS) No. 218; the two main types are three-quarter and full-face.
A helmet should fit snugly, show no defects such as cracks, frayed straps, loose padding, or exposed metal, and be securely fastened every time you ride.

A full, shatter-resistant faceshield (VESC-8 in the manual) protects best; goggles protect only the eyes. For safety, a windshield is no substitute for either, even though the law on page 9 lets an operator skip eye protection if the bike has a windshield or screen.
Don't wear tinted eye protection at night or at any other time when light is low.
Jackets and pants should fully cover arms and legs, boots should cover the ankles, and gloves should be leather or a durable synthetic.

Wear a jacket even on warm days to prevent dehydration. In cold or wet weather, dress to stay warm and dry; being numb from the cold hurts control, and long cold rides can lead to severe chill, fatigue, or even hypothermia.
Do a complete pre-ride check every time: tires, fluids, lights, turn signals, clutch and throttle, mirrors, brakes (one at a time), and horn.
On an unfamiliar or borrowed bike, check all controls, learn the gear pattern, and ride cautiously until you know how it handles.

questions.q: Under Massachusetts law, what color must the headlight on the front of a motorcycle be?
options: Amber
White
Red
Yellow
questions.explanation: The manual requires a properly aimed white headlight on the front of the motorcycle.

questions.q: Which set of lights must the rear of a motorcycle have?
options: A white taillight, a stoplight, and a red license plate light
A white taillight and a stoplight; a plate light is optional
A red taillight, a stoplight, and a white license plate light
An amber taillight, a stoplight, and a white license plate light
questions.explanation: At the rear, the manual requires a red taillight, a stoplight, and a white lamp that shines on the license plate.

questions.q: How high may motorcycle handlebars be in Massachusetts?
options: No higher than the operator's shoulders when properly seated
No higher than the top of the operator's helmet when seated
No higher than 15 inches above the top of the operator's seat
Any height, as long as the operator can reach the grips
questions.explanation: Handlebars must not rise above the operator's shoulders when the operator is seated properly. That is the legal limit; separately, page 16 advises setting the bars so your hands are level with or below your elbows.

questions.q: If a motorcycle is equipped to carry passengers, what must it have?
options: A passenger backrest and sturdy grab handles on both sides
A secure passenger seat and separate passenger footpegs
A sidecar or a trailer hitch to carry the added weight
A second set of rearview mirrors and a louder horn
questions.explanation: A motorcycle that carries passengers needs a secure seat for them and separate footpegs.

questions.q: Who is required to wear a helmet on a motorcycle in Massachusetts?
options: Only operators and passengers under 18
The operator, but not a passenger
Everyone except adults over 21 with health insurance
Both the operator and any passenger
questions.explanation: Massachusetts law makes helmet use mandatory for motorcycle riders and passengers alike.

questions.q: According to the manual, about how often is a motorcycle helmet effective in preventing brain injury?
options: 33% of the time
50% of the time
67% of the time
90% of the time
questions.explanation: The manual says that although a helmet can't prevent many other kinds of injury, it is effective in preventing brain injury about 67 percent of the time.

questions.q: Motorcycle helmets sold in the United States must meet which standard?
options: Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard No. 218
Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard No. 108
VESC-8
SAE J1100
questions.explanation: The manual says every motorcycle helmet sold in the U.S. must meet FMVSS No. 218, the performance standard that sets a helmet's minimum level of protection.

questions.q: What are the two main types of motorcycle helmets described in the manual?
options: Half-shell and modular
Three-quarter and full-face
Fiberglass and polycarbonate
Motocross and touring
questions.explanation: The manual names three-quarter and full-face helmets as the two types, each offering a different level of coverage.

questions.q: Before buying a used helmet, what should you first make sure of?
options: That it is less than two years old, based on its date of manufacture
That it comes with a tinted visor for bright daytime riding
That it has never been worn by a passenger, only by an operator
That its manufacturer or distributor will re-inspect it for damage
questions.explanation: Helmet damage is not always visible, so the manual advises confirming the maker or distributor will re-inspect a used helmet.

questions.q: Which type of eye and face protection does the manual recommend for the best protection?
options: A full, shatter-resistant faceshield
A tall windshield that reaches eye level
Well-fitted, shatter-resistant goggles
Prescription eyeglasses with side shields
questions.explanation: The manual recommends a full faceshield because it protects the whole face, not just the eyes; goggles, glasses, and windshields all give less protection.

questions.q: For protecting your eyes and face, which statement about windshields is correct according to the manual?
options: A windshield protects your eyes just as well as goggles do
Most windshields will keep the wind out of a rider's eyes
A windshield is not a substitute for a faceshield or goggles
A windshield gives more protection than a full faceshield
questions.explanation: A windshield can't take the place of a faceshield or goggles, and most windshields won't keep wind out of your eyes. That is safety advice: the legal rule on page 9 lets an operator skip eye protection if the bike has a windshield or screen.

questions.q: When should tinted eye protection NOT be worn?
options: In bright midday sun with strong glare
At night or whenever little light is available
At highway speeds, where the wind is strongest
When riding through heavy daytime city traffic
questions.explanation: Tint cuts the light reaching your eyes, so the manual says not to wear it at night or in other low-light conditions.

questions.q: Which is a requirement for effective eye and faceshield protection?
options: It must be tinted dark enough to cut the glare from other vehicles
It must seal tightly against the face so no air passes through
It must be free of scratches and give a clear view to either side
It must fit so closely that eyeglasses cannot be worn under it
questions.explanation: Effective eye and face protection must be scratch-free and give a clear view to the sides; it must also let air through to limit fogging and leave room for glasses if you need them.

questions.q: According to the manual, what should riding boots or shoes be like?
options: High enough to cover the ankles, with hard, durable, slip-resistant soles
Low-cut, below the ankles, with thin soles to give a better feel of the pegs
Soft, flexible soles and tall heels that hook securely on the footpegs
Loosely laced, with long laces left outside so they are easy to adjust
questions.explanation: Footwear should cover and support the ankles, have tough slip-resistant soles, short heels, and tucked-in laces.

questions.q: During a pre-ride check, how should you test the brakes?
options: Apply both brakes together while rolling slowly and check that the bike stops straight
Try the front and rear brakes one at a time; each should feel firm and hold the bike
Pump only the rear brake until it feels firm, since the front brake needs no check
Don't test them; brakes only need checking when the motorcycle is inspected
questions.explanation: The checklist says to test each brake separately and confirm it is firm and holds the bike when fully applied.

questions.q: You are about to ride a borrowed motorcycle. What does the manual advise?
options: Skip the usual safety checks, since the owner is responsible for keeping it maintained
Do your usual checks, then ride at your normal pace and following distance
Check the controls, learn the gear pattern, and ride very cautiously until familiar with it
Don't bother checking the controls, since they work the same way on every motorcycle
questions.explanation: On an unfamiliar bike, do all your usual checks and learn the controls and shift pattern. Then ride more carefully than usual, not at your normal pace: accelerate gently, slow more for turns, and leave extra room until you know how it handles.

questions.q: Per mile traveled, how does a motorcycle rider's chance of dying in a traffic crash compare with a car passenger's, according to the manual?
options: The two are about equally likely to die
The car passenger is more likely to die
The motorcycle rider is more likely to die
The rider is more likely to die, but only without a helmet
questions.explanation: Citing the U.S. Department of Transportation and NHTSA, the manual says that mile for mile, motorcycle riders are more likely than car passengers to die in a crash. Riding with an approved helmet, eye and face protection, and protective clothing greatly improves your odds of avoiding serious injury.

questions.q: According to NHTSA figures cited in the manual, how many motorcyclists' lives does helmet use save each year?
options: A few dozen
Hundreds
Tens of thousands
Almost none, since helmets mainly prevent minor injuries
questions.explanation: The manual cites NHTSA's finding that wearing helmets saves hundreds of motorcyclists' lives each year. Don't mix this up with the manual's other figure, thousands of injuries in motorcycle crashes in a single year.

questions.q: In the manual, the standard VESC-8 is linked to which piece of gear?
options: A motorcycle helmet
A plastic shatter-resistant faceshield
Leather or synthetic riding gloves
A windshield mounted on the motorcycle
questions.explanation: The manual tags a plastic shatter-resistant faceshield with VESC-8. Such a shield can protect your whole face in a crash and blocks wind, dust, rain, insects and pebbles kicked up by traffic ahead.

questions.q: How often does the manual recommend making a complete check of your motorcycle?
options: Once a week
Before every ride
Once a month
Only before long trips
questions.explanation: Motorcycles need attention more often than other vehicles, so the manual strongly recommends a complete check before each ride to catch a mechanical defect or equipment failure.
